title: Muscle, Bone, and Joint Histology
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the microscopic structure of the musculoskeletal system: the sarcomere, the three muscle types, compact and spongy bone, the cells that build and remove bone, the epiphyseal growth plate, and the three classes of joints. Board questions rarely ask for a label alone. They ask you to predict what changes when a filament slides, a receptor is overactive, a mineral is missing, or a tissue has no blood supply. Each structure here is explained by the job it does, so that achondroplasia, rickets, osteopetrosis, and cartilage that heals poorly follow directly from normal histology.
prerequisites: Basic tissue types and the structure of collagen and proteoglycans
Cell junctions: gap junctions, desmosomes, and adherens junctions
Calcium and phosphate balance with PTH and vitamin D (EN-5)

terms.def: The contractile unit of striated muscle, extending from one Z line to the next.
A T tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum, found at the A band to I band junction in skeletal muscle.
The step-shaped junction between cardiac muscle cells that contains fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions.
A cytoplasmic or membrane-attached plaque rich in alpha-actinin that anchors thin filaments in smooth muscle, the functional equivalent of a Z line.
The structural unit of compact bone: concentric lamellae arranged around a central (Haversian) canal.
Newly secreted, unmineralized bone matrix, mostly type I collagen.
A ligand on osteoblast-lineage cells that binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and drives their formation and activation.
A soluble decoy receptor made by osteoblasts that binds RANKL and prevents osteoclast activation.
The shallow pit on a bone surface that an active osteoclast excavates beneath its ruffled border.
The disc of hyaline cartilage between epiphysis and metaphysis whose chondrocytes drive lengthening of long bones.
A primary cartilaginous joint in which bones are joined by hyaline cartilage.
A secondary cartilaginous joint in which bones are joined by fibrocartilage, usually in the midline.

blocks.text: Skeletal and cardiac muscle look striated because their myofibrils are built of repeating sarcomeres lined up in register across the cell. A sarcomere runs from one Z line (Z disc) to the next. Thin filaments of actin, with tropomyosin and troponin, are anchored at the Z line by alpha-actinin and project toward the center. Thick filaments of myosin sit in the center, held in place at the M line and tethered to the Z line by the giant elastic protein titin.

The bands are defined by which filaments are present. The A band (anisotropic: birefringent in polarized light, dark in stained sections) is the full length of the thick filaments, including the parts that overlap thin filaments. The I band (isotropic, light) contains thin filaments only and is bisected by the Z line, so each I band belongs to two neighboring sarcomeres. The H zone is the central part of the A band where thick filaments are not overlapped by thin filaments, and the M line runs through its middle, where proteins such as myomesin cross-link the thick filaments.

blocks.title: Sarcomere landmarks and what happens to them
rows: Alpha-actinin anchoring thin filaments; sarcomere boundary
Cross-linking proteins in the center of the thick filaments
blocks.caption: Only regions defined by the absence of overlap change length; the A band is set by the length of the thick filament itself.

blocks.text: These changes follow from the sliding filament mechanism. Neither actin nor myosin filaments change length. Myosin heads on each half of the bipolar thick filament pull their thin filaments toward the M line, so overlap increases. The non-overlap regions (I band and H zone) therefore narrow, the Z lines approach each other, and the A band is unchanged. When a muscle is passively stretched the opposite occurs: the I band and H zone widen while the A band still stays constant.

blocks.title: Calculating band widths
blocks.text: Take thick filaments of about 1.6 micrometers and thin filaments of about 1.0 micrometer extending from each Z line, ignoring Z line thickness. At a sarcomere length of 2.4 micrometers, the A band is 1.6, the I band is 2.4 minus 1.6, or 0.8, and the H zone is 2.4 minus 2 times 1.0, or 0.4. If the sarcomere shortens to 2.0 micrometers, the A band is still 1.6, the I band falls to 0.4, and the H zone falls to 0. The I band and H zone each lost 0.4 micrometers, exactly the amount the sarcomere shortened, because the thin filaments slid that distance.

The amount of overlap also sets force. Near the length where every myosin head can reach actin and thin filaments do not collide, tension is maximal; at very long lengths few cross-bridges form, and at very short lengths filaments collide and interfere. This length-tension relationship (MS-7) is the sarcomere basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism in the heart.

blocks.predict: A muscle fiber is stretched passively well beyond its resting length. Which bands change, and in which direction?
blocks.explain: The I band and H zone widen because the thin filaments are pulled out of overlap, and the Z lines move apart. The A band does not change because thick filament length does not change.

sections.title: Skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle on histology

blocks.text: Each muscle type is built around how it receives its signal to contract and how its cells work together. Recognizing them on a slide comes down to four questions: is the tissue striated, where are the nuclei, how many are there, and how are the cells joined.

A skeletal muscle fiber is a single huge cell formed by fusion of myoblasts, so it is multinucleate, with many nuclei pressed flat against the sarcolemma. In cross section fibers are polygonal with peripheral nuclei. Because each fiber is wide and must contract uniformly along its length, T tubules (inward extensions of the sarcolemma) dive into the fiber at every A band to I band junction and pair with two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum to form triads, giving rapid, uniform calcium release. Mature fiber nuclei do not divide; repair depends on satellite cells lying between the sarcolemma and the basal lamina. Centrally placed nuclei in skeletal muscle are therefore abnormal and indicate regeneration or a myopathy.

Cardiac muscle cells are separate cells that must contract as one unit. They are branched, with one or occasionally two central nuclei, often surrounded by a pale perinuclear zone that collects lipofuscin with age. Intercalated discs join cells end to end. Their transverse portions carry fascia adherens, which anchor actin filaments, and desmosomes, which link desmin intermediate filaments and keep cells from pulling apart; their lateral portions carry gap junctions (mainly connexin 43) that let depolarization spread from cell to cell so the myocardium behaves as a functional syncytium. Cardiac T tubules are wider and lie at the Z lines, usually pairing with a single SR cisterna as a dyad, which fits the cardiac reliance on calcium entering through L-type channels to trigger SR calcium release. Adult cardiomyocytes have very limited capacity to divide, so injury heals by fibrous scar and increased workload causes hypertrophy.

Smooth muscle cells are fusiform with one central, cigar-shaped nucleus that may look corkscrewed in a contracted cell. Actin and myosin are not arranged in register, so there are no striations; thin filaments attach to dense bodies in the cytoplasm and on the membrane, and desmin intermediate filaments link the dense bodies into a network that pulls the cell into a shorter, rounder shape. There are no T tubules; caveolae and a sparse SR serve the small cell. Single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle is coupled by gap junctions. Smooth muscle can divide, so organs such as the uterus in pregnancy enlarge by both hypertrophy and hyperplasia.

rows: Intercalated discs: fascia adherens, desmosomes, gap junctions
Triads at A to I junction
Dyads at Z line, wider T tubules
blocks.caption: Peripheral nuclei plus striations means skeletal; central nuclei plus striations and intercalated discs means cardiac; central nucleus without striations means smooth.

sections.title: Compact bone, spongy bone, and woven versus lamellar bone

blocks.text: Bone matrix is type I collagen hardened by hydroxyapatite crystals. Mineral gives stiffness and collagen gives resistance to fracture, but mineralized matrix blocks diffusion, so every osteocyte must stay within a short distance of a blood vessel. The architecture of bone is largely the solution to that supply problem.

Compact (cortical) bone forms the shafts of long bones and the outer shell of all bones. Its unit is the osteon (Haversian system), a cylinder of concentric lamellae running along the long axis of the bone around a central Haversian canal that carries capillaries and nerves. Collagen fibers in adjacent lamellae run in alternating directions, which resists loads from several directions. Osteocytes sit in lacunae between lamellae and extend processes through tiny channels called canaliculi; the processes meet through gap junctions, so nutrients and signals pass from the central canal outward cell by cell. Volkmann (perforating) canals run across the bone, roughly perpendicular to osteons, and connect Haversian canals to each other, to the periosteum, and to the marrow cavity; they are not surrounded by concentric lamellae. Each osteon is bounded by a cement line. Between osteons lie interstitial lamellae, the remnants of older, partly resorbed osteons, and circumferential lamellae line the outer and inner surfaces.

The periosteum covers the outer surface. Its outer fibrous layer is anchored by collagen (Sharpey) fibers, and its inner layer holds osteoprogenitor cells that allow growth in width and fracture repair. A thinner endosteum lines the marrow cavity and trabeculae.

Spongy (cancellous, trabecular) bone, found in vertebral bodies, the ends of long bones, and the interior of flat bones, is a lattice of thin plates and struts called trabeculae with marrow in the spaces between them. Trabeculae are thin enough to be nourished from the marrow surface, so they lack osteons and Haversian canals. Their large surface area makes trabecular bone turn over faster than cortical bone, which is why trabecular-rich sites such as vertebrae, the distal radius, and the femoral neck lose mass early in osteoporosis.

blocks.title: Woven versus lamellar bone
rows: Nearly all of the adult skeleton
Paget disease, fibrous dysplasia, bone tumors, severe hyperparathyroidism
blocks.caption: Woven bone trades strength for speed and is normally remodeled into lamellar bone; its presence in adult bone signals rapid abnormal formation.

blocks.text: Paget disease shows why the distinction matters. Disordered, excessive osteoclast resorption followed by disorganized osteoblast repair forms woven bone early and later a mosaic of lamellar bone with irregular cement lines, so the bone is thicker yet weaker and prone to bowing and fracture.
Bone is remodeled throughout life. Formation and resorption are coupled because the osteoblast lineage controls the osteoclast, and most hormones that change bone mass act at that point.

Osteoblasts arise from mesenchymal stem cells under the transcription factors RUNX2 and osterix, with Wnt and beta-catenin signaling promoting their differentiation. They are cuboidal cells with basophilic cytoplasm, rich in rough ER, lining bone surfaces. They secrete osteoid, which is mostly type I collagen with noncollagenous proteins such as osteocalcin, and they express alkaline phosphatase, which raises local phosphate and breaks down pyrophosphate, an inhibitor of mineralization, so hydroxyapatite can form in the osteoid. Serum bone-specific alkaline phosphatase therefore rises when bone formation is active, as in growth, fracture healing, Paget disease, and rickets. Osteoblasts carry the PTH receptor and vitamin D receptor and secrete both RANKL and OPG.

Osteocytes are osteoblasts walled in by their own matrix; they are the most numerous bone cells and connect through canaliculi. Fluid flow in the canaliculi during loading lets them act as mechanosensors. Unloading increases their secretion of sclerostin, which inhibits Wnt signaling in osteoblasts and reduces formation, while loading suppresses sclerostin. Osteocytes are also the main source of FGF23, which lowers serum phosphate (see the cycle below).

Osteoclasts come from the monocyte and macrophage lineage, not from mesenchyme. M-CSF and RANKL drive precursors to fuse into large multinucleated cells with acidophilic cytoplasm. An active osteoclast seals onto bone with integrin alpha-v beta-3 at a ring-shaped sealing zone. Inside the ring, its ruffled border pumps H+ through a vacuolar H+ ATPase, with H+ supplied by carbonic anhydrase II and chloride following through the ClC-7 channel; the resulting acid dissolves hydroxyapatite, and the protease cathepsin K then digests the exposed collagen. The pit left behind is a Howship lacuna. Osteoclasts express tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) and calcitonin receptors.

blocks.title: Coupled remodeling
steps: PTH or local signals raise RANKL relative to OPG
RANKL binds RANK on monocyte-lineage precursors (with M-CSF)
Ruffled border releases acid and cathepsin K
Howship lacuna forms; matrix factors recruit osteoblasts
Osteoblasts lay osteoid that then mineralizes
Some osteoblasts are trapped and become osteocytes
blocks.caption: PTH acts on osteoblast-lineage cells, which signal osteoclast precursors through RANKL; osteoclasts lack PTH receptors.

blocks.title: Osteocyte FGF23 and phosphate
steps: FGF23 also lowers 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so calcitriol falls
Serum phosphate falls, reducing FGF23 drive
blocks.caption: Excess FGF23, as in X-linked hypophosphatemia from PHEX mutation, causes renal phosphate wasting and rickets or osteomalacia.

blocks.text: This control explains several classic findings. Continuously high PTH raises RANKL relative to OPG and causes net resorption, whereas estrogen restrains RANKL signaling and shortens osteoclast life, so its loss at menopause speeds resorption. If osteoclasts cannot acidify their lacuna, bone is not removed, producing osteopetrosis: dense, brittle bone that crowds the marrow and narrows cranial foramina. Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency adds renal tubular acidosis, and cathepsin K deficiency causes pycnodysostosis.

blocks.predict: A mouse lacks the gene for osteoprotegerin. What happens to its bone mass, and why?
blocks.explain: Bone mass falls. Without the decoy receptor, RANKL binds RANK unopposed, so osteoclast formation and resorption outpace formation.
blocks.check: The RANKL and OPG steps in the remodeling flow.

blocks.title: Dense bones that break
blocks.text: A child has fractures after minor falls, anemia, metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately high urine pH, and uniformly dense bones on radiographs. Dense bone means bone is made but not removed, so osteoclasts are failing. The marrow cavity shrinks, causing anemia, and old microdamaged matrix is never replaced, so bone is dense but brittle. A defect shared by bone and renal tubules points to the enzyme both use to generate secreted H+: carbonic anhydrase II. The diagnosis is osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis from carbonic anhydrase II deficiency.

sections.title: The epiphyseal growth plate, achondroplasia, and rickets

blocks.text: Long bones lengthen by endochondral ossification at the growth plate (physis), a disc of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and the metaphysis. Bone does not grow by expansion of existing bone; cartilage is added on the epiphyseal side and replaced by bone on the metaphyseal side. The plate keeps a fairly constant thickness during growth because the two processes run at matched rates.

blocks.title: Growth plate zones, epiphysis to diaphysis
steps: Reserve zone: scattered resting chondrocytes supply new cells
Proliferative zone: chondrocytes divide into stacked columns
Hypertrophic zone: cells swell, make type X collagen and VEGF
Calcification zone: matrix mineralizes, chondrocytes die
Ossification zone: vessels invade, osteoblasts lay bone on cartilage
blocks.caption: Proliferation and hypertrophy produce length; mineralization of cartilage and vascular invasion let bone replace it.

blocks.text: Length comes from two steps: division in the proliferative zone and enlargement of chondrocytes in the hypertrophic zone, which accounts for much of the gain. Hypertrophic chondrocytes release VEGF and matrix vesicles; once their matrix calcifies they die, and the calcified cartilage becomes a scaffold. Capillaries and osteoprogenitor cells from the marrow invade, and osteoblasts deposit bone on the calcified cartilage, producing mixed spicules with a cartilage core and a bone covering that are later remodeled. Proliferation is regulated by growth hormone through IGF-1, thyroid hormone, a local Indian hedgehog and PTHrP feedback loop, and FGFR3 signaling, which acts as a brake. Estrogen in both sexes eventually closes the plate. The hypertrophic zone, with large cells and little matrix, is the mechanically weakest layer, so physeal fractures and slipped capital femoral epiphysis usually pass through it.

Achondroplasia is a gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3, autosomal dominant but usually a new mutation, often linked to advanced paternal age. The overactive receptor suppresses chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy, so the proliferative zone is thin with short, disorganized columns. Bones formed by endochondral ossification are short, especially the proximal limb segments, while bones formed by intramembranous ossification, such as the skull vault, grow normally. The result is short limbs with a near-normal trunk, a relatively large head with frontal bossing, and a small cranial base that can narrow the foramen magnum.

Rickets is defective mineralization of the growing skeleton, from vitamin D deficiency or from phosphate loss. Low phosphate prevents the normal apoptosis of hypertrophic chondrocytes, and unmineralized cartilage cannot be invaded by vessels and replaced. Hypertrophic chondrocytes therefore pile up in long, disordered columns, the plate becomes wide and irregular, and osteoid accumulates without mineral. Radiographs show widened plates with frayed, cupped metaphyses. Clinically, enlarged costochondral junctions form the rachitic rosary, and soft bones bow under weight bearing. In adults, whose plates have closed, the same mineral defect causes osteomalacia, with excess osteoid on bone surfaces but no plate changes.

blocks.title: Growth plate in achondroplasia and rickets
rows: Too little mineralization (low vitamin D or phosphate)
blocks.caption: Achondroplasia makes too little cartilage; rickets makes cartilage that cannot be converted to bone.

blocks.text: Joints are classified by the tissue that binds the bones together, and that tissue determines how much movement is possible. Fibrous joints are joined by dense connective tissue and move little, cartilaginous joints by cartilage and move slightly, and synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity and move freely.

blocks.title: Joint classes
rows: Allow molding at birth and skull growth; may fuse with age
Distal tibiofibular joint; radius and ulna interosseous membrane
Epiphyseal plate; spheno-occipital; first sternocostal joint
Fibrocartilage, with thin hyaline cartilage on the bone ends
Pubic symphysis; intervertebral disc; manubriosternal joint
Joint capsule enclosing a synovial cavity
blocks.caption: Synchondroses use hyaline cartilage and symphyses use fibrocartilage.

blocks.text: Fibrocartilage combines rows of chondrocytes with dense bundles of type I collagen in addition to type II, so it resists both compression and tension, suiting it to the pubic symphysis and the annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc. The disc's central nucleus pulposus is a gel derived from the notochord. When the annulus weakens, usually posterolaterally where the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow, the nucleus can herniate and compress a nerve root.

A synovial joint is enclosed by a capsule with an outer fibrous layer and an inner synovial membrane. The synovium has no true epithelium and no basement membrane: one to a few layers of synoviocytes rest on vascular loose connective tissue. Type A synoviocytes are macrophage-like cells derived from bone marrow that clear debris; type B synoviocytes are fibroblast-like cells that secrete hyaluronan and lubricin. Synovial fluid is a filtrate of plasma enriched with these molecules. Hyaluronan makes the fluid viscous, and lubricin coats the cartilage surface to reduce friction.

Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage rich in type II collagen and aggrecan, whose negatively charged glycosaminoglycans hold water and resist compression. Unlike most hyaline cartilage it has no perichondrium, and it has no blood vessels, lymphatics, or nerves. Chondrocytes receive nutrients by diffusion from synovial fluid, helped by the pumping effect of cyclic loading. With no vessels to bring repair cells and no perichondrium to supply new chondroblasts, damaged articular cartilage repairs poorly, which underlies osteoarthritis. In rheumatoid arthritis, by contrast, the disease begins in the vascular synovium, which proliferates into a pannus that erodes cartilage and bone.

blocks.predict: A full-thickness defect in articular cartilage reaches the subchondral bone. How will it heal compared with a defect confined to the cartilage?
blocks.explain: A defect limited to cartilage barely heals because no vessels or perichondrium can supply repair cells. A defect reaching subchondral bone lets marrow cells and blood enter, but they form fibrocartilage, which is weaker and wears faster than hyaline cartilage.
blocks.check: The paragraph on articular cartilage nutrition and repair.

integration.text: Embryology and histology set the pattern. Endochondral bones grow from a cartilage model at growth plates while intramembranous bones form directly in mesenchyme, which is why FGFR3 mutations shorten limbs but spare the skull vault. Muscle structure mirrors its signaling: triads, dyads, and caveolae match how each muscle type raises cytosolic calcium (MS-7, CV-5), and the ability to divide (smooth muscle), regenerate from satellite cells (skeletal), or only scar (cardiac) predicts the outcome of injury.

Physiology, biochemistry, and pathology meet at the bone cell. Bone mass reflects the balance of RANKL and OPG on osteoblast-lineage cells, with PTH, estrogen, and mechanical load acting there; mineralization depends on vitamin D, phosphate, FGF23, and alkaline phosphatase; and collagen types I and II determine the behavior of bone and cartilage. Histology explains appearance and mechanism but not every clinical detail, because the same pattern can have several causes: a wide growth plate is rickets from vitamin D deficiency or from renal phosphate wasting, and only serum chemistry separates them.

summary: During contraction the I band, H zone, and sarcomere shorten while the A band, set by thick filament length, stays constant; no filament changes length.

Skeletal muscle is multinucleate with peripheral nuclei and triads; cardiac muscle is branched with central nuclei, dyads, and intercalated discs; smooth muscle is fusiform, nonstriated, and anchors actin to dense bodies.
Intercalated disc gap junctions make the myocardium a functional syncytium, while fascia adherens and desmosomes hold cells together.
Compact bone osteons keep osteocytes near Haversian vessels through canaliculi and gap junctions; Volkmann canals cross between osteons.
Spongy bone has no osteons and a large surface area, so it turns over faster and is lost first in osteoporosis; woven bone in adults signals abnormal rapid formation.
Osteoblasts (mesenchymal) make type I collagen osteoid and alkaline phosphatase and control osteoclasts through RANKL and OPG; osteocytes sense load and secrete sclerostin and FGF23.
Osteoclasts (monocyte lineage) dissolve mineral with acid from carbonic anhydrase II and digest collagen with cathepsin K in Howship lacunae; failure causes osteopetrosis.
Growth plate zones run reserve, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcification, ossification; achondroplasia thins the proliferative zone and rickets widens a disordered hypertrophic zone.
Fibrous joints are sutures, syndesmoses, and gomphoses; synchondroses are hyaline and symphyses are fibrocartilage.
Articular cartilage lacks vessels and perichondrium and is fed by synovial fluid, whose hyaluronan and lubricin come from type B synoviocytes, so it repairs poorly.

The manubriosternal joint is usually classed as a symphysis but can ossify in older adults; confirm whether NABNE lists it.
Confirm whether NABNE expects type A and type B synoviocyte terminology and the protein name lubricin (proteoglycan 4).
The statement that osteoclasts lack PTH receptors reflects the standard teaching consensus; some research reports low-level expression.
